item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

23 Sep 2026, 07:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Butler II)
Nathaniel Lowe hit a sacrifice fly to right field that drove in Chase DeLauter in the ninth inning and the visiting Cleveland Guardians held on to beat the Boston Red Sox 3-2 Tuesday in the first game of a three-game series.
Boston's Erik Miller (4-2) walked one and allowed two hits in the ninth.
Hunter Gaddis (5-3) got the win despite allowing a game-tying home run to Mickey Gasper in the eighth. Cade Smith pitched a scoreless ninth to record his 40th save. The victory extended Cleveland's winning streak to six games as it maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings. He struck out five and walked one. Messick has allowed three runs or fewer in each of his last 14 starts.
Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox (84-73) and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings. He walked two and struck out five.
Adley Rutschman had three hits for the Red Sox, who had eight hits in the game.
Cleveland's Angel Martinez went 3-for-4 and scored a run. The Guardians (82-75) received two hits from DeLauter, who reached in the ninth when Miller hit him with a pitch.
The Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
The Guardians took a 2-0 lead in the second. Martinez doubled and made it 1-0 when he scored on David Fry's single. Fry doubled the lead by scoring when Brayan Rocchio grounded into a 4-6-3 double play.
Boston trimmed its deficit to 2-1 in the second. Rutschman led off with a double, moved to third on Caleb Durbin's groundout to second and scored on Andrew Monasterio's groundout to shortstop.
Gasper's home run, his 10th of the year, tied the game leading off the eighth.
Boston stranded the tying run on second in the ninth as Smith retired Nick Sogard on a grounder to second.

After an off day on Monday, the Boston Red Sox will return to Fenway Park to begin the next-to-last series of the regular season before the playoffs next week. Boston clinched their spot in the postseason after the Atlanta Braves completed a three-game sweep of the Houston Astros on Sunday afternoon.
The Red Sox are all but locked into the second American League wild-card spot. They are on a collision course with the New York Yankees next week in the Bronx for a best-of-three series. Before then, however, Boston has three games with the Cleveland Guardians. They will then host the Chicago Cubs this weekend, weather permitting.
As for the Guardians series, Wilyer Abreu is back in the lineup for manager Chad Tracy and batting in a familiar spot.
Boston Red Sox Announce Wilyer Abreu Spot in Lineup Against Guardians on Tuesday Night
Tracy will send left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound to open the series and as far as his lineup goes, Abreu us back and batting cleanup. Here is Boston's lineup for the series opener against Cleveland's Parker Messick,
Nick Sogard 1B
Jahmai Jones DH
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caleb Durbin 3B
Isiah Kiner-Falefa SS
Nate Eaton CF
Abreu will be batting fourth, with first baseman Willson Contreras still out of the lineup after getting hit by a pitch last Thursday night against the Texas Rangers. He missed the series against the Tampa Bay Rays. As for Abreu, he did not play in Sunday's series finale, a 5-1 loss.
Boston Red Sox Playing Out the String Ahead of Playoffs
Tuesday, it was announced that Tracy was having the interim tag removed, and Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow is having his option in 2029 and 2030 picked up by the club. It's not surprising that it was announced before the playoffs.
Boston is scheduled to send their three projected starters on the mound next week against the Yankees: Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez against the Guardians. However, Cleveland is in a heated race with the Chicago White Sox for the American League Central Division title. They enter the series with a one-game lead over the White Sox, who are playing the Kansas City Royals this week.
Boston has slumped in September. However, they can use the six games before next week as a tune-up. As for this weekend, the weather is projected to be a mess. Tim Healy of the Boston Globe reported that MLB has no plans to move the series out of Boston. There are going to be very few windows to play baseball this weekend.
The Cubs are in a battle for home-field advantage in the National League wild-card round. Those games will have big meaning for them and the NL. They enter play this week tied with the San Diego Padres for home-field advantage next week. The Philadelphia Phillies are a game behind. There is a lot riding on this weekend.

item.content:encoded:
The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.content:encoded:
After a rollercoaster of a season which included a brutal start, sudden managerial firings, historic win streaks and a playoff clinch, the Boston Red Sox have extended the man who brought it all together. Boston has removed Chad Tracy's "interim" tag and made him their manager, first reported by Christopher Smith of MassLive.
Tracy and the Red Sox have agreed to a three-year contract with a club option in 2030, per Smith. His salary has not yet been reported.
Tracy was Boston's Triple-A manager on April 25, the day Alex Cora and six other members of his coaching staff were fired. The Red Sox then flew him out to Baltimore to take over in a whirlwind and a leap of faith, and it worked. He'll be the 49th manager in Red Sox franchise history (subscription required).
The Red Sox had a 10-17 record on the day of Tracy's promotion and he managed the club to two games below .500 by July 12, the start of the All-Star break. Boston's historic 15-game winning streak had already begun by then — it rallied to sweep the New York Yankees in four games two weeks before, lost a series to the Washington Nationals, and it was all winning from there.
Red Sox name Chad Tracy manager through 2029, exercised club options to keep Craig Breslow CBO through 2030
Tracy had long been revered as the manager of the WooSox and it didn't take long for Red Sox fans to become equally endeared to him. His direct, but friendly communication style offered a stark contrast to other leaders in the organization. He had preexisting relationships with many of the organization's young players from their time in Triple-A and from rehab assignments, and it showed. After the Red Sox's historic July and August spell, Tracy's promotion seemed almost inevitable, and rightfully so.
Within the Tracy contract announcement, the Red Sox also included another contract update. The Red Sox have exercised the 2029-30 club options on Craig Breslow's contract, essentially extending him for another two years.
This is quite a sign of trust from Boston. Breslow's tenure started with some massive moves like the Garrett Crochet trade, and the Red Sox made the playoffs for the first time in three seasons with him at the helm. But his communication style has been criticized, it's led to massive trades of players who were supposed to be fixtiures of the organization for years to come, and front office leaks have marred his public image.
But Breslow has loosened up a bit since the beginning of the season. He's been pictured around the players more often and has been cracking jokes on his radio appearances.
There's also no denying that he had a great 2025-26 offseason. Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Ranger Suarez and Caleb Durbin, all acquired by Breslow over the offseason, are all major parts of the Red Sox's success.
Cora had been Boston's manager for eight seasons and many Red Sox fans couldn't stand Breslow at the beginning of June. Things can change quickly in baseball.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.

Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

It’s not remotely the right time to start talking about offseason movement, but there is movement afoot. Two of Craig Breslow’s assistant GMs, Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith, have already conducted preliminary interviews for the big chair in Sacramento after the A’s fired Dave Forst back in August. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Here in Boston, though, we’re unlikely to see a search for a new boss in a while. Craig Breslow earned himself quite a bit of rope this season, thanks to a decisive move that paid off big time in firing Alex Cora. “I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said. “And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
And here’ s a look at some of the key moments of the season that got this team where it is today. Remember the ninth inning comeback against the Mets that came after that long-delayed flight? How about Caleb Durbin’s home run off Cam Schlittler? (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
But, strangely enough, when it came time to clinch the playoffs, it wasn’t a Red Sox player who did the dirty work, though it was a Red Sox legacy player. “And the man with the game-winning three-run homer that would, in the end, send both the Braves and the Red Sox to the postseason? Well, baseball is quite sentimental, and it also has a sense of humor, so, obviously, it was Mike Yastrzemski.“ (Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, MLB.com)
But the fact that the Sox clinched on a loss didn’t dampen the celebration. “There was a lot of beer!” said Payton Tolle. “It was a slobberknocker.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
But before the slobberknocker could get slobbin’, Chad Tracy addressed his team to sum up the season that was. “I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room,” he said. “I’m so grateful for you guys, for our staff, for everybody. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, ‘The hell with that, we’re going to the playoffs.’ And you did.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
So the Sox are in the dance. But for how long? That’s anyone’s guess, but Red Sox fans are apparently more optimistic than the fans of any other American league team. (Stephen J. Nesbitt, The Athletic)

The Boston Red Sox secured their spot in the postseason thanks to an Atlanta Braves win over the Houston Astros.
Things are going well now, but Red Sox fans remember the 10-17 start that led to Alex Cora and six other coaches being fired. Since then, interim manager Chad Tracy has led the charge in turning things around, but it has not all been him. The players started living up to expectations, and the team has gotten healthy.
At the time, many questioned Craig Breslow's ability to make decisions, with many fans saying Cora was fired as a result of Breslow failing to address the team's biggest flaws in the offseason. However, now it looks like Breslow was right to trust his players.
"I believed in the players that we had,” Breslow said when asked about the move to fire Cora, per The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey. “I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive. And they responded. While there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly.”
One example of Breslow's belief paying off is Caleb Durbin. Durbin was acquired to replace Alex Bregman, and he was a terrible hitter through two months. However, after back-to-back off days in May, he has been on another level. He is looking more like the Rookie of the Year finalist he was for the Milwaukee Brewers last year. He looks like a real player the Red Sox can rely on down the line.
Perhaps what's most impressive about this Red Sox team is that they have turned the season around without arguably their two best pitchers, Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony. However, Anthony is back, and Crochet could be in the bullpen for October.

In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith.
Nearly halfway through the season, at the bottom of a bad American League, in a sport dominated by data and measurables, virtually all available evidence led to a consistent conclusion: The 2026 Red Sox were just not good. They fired the manager a month in. They lost key players to long-term injuries. They showed little life.
And so they were left with mere belief. Belief in themselves, belief that they could salvage it, belief that how could it possibly stay like this forever?
“We all still had faith in each other,” Garrett Whitlock said. “Human beings still do the thing. All the numbers and data would have counted us out and all that kind of stuff. And the players in this clubhouse were like, hey, we can stick with this.”
Or, at least, that’s what they said.
“We wouldn’t have said it if we didn’t believe it,” Caleb Durbin said.
Improbably, incredibly, here they are. They clinched a spot in the postseason Sunday, allowing aspirations of late October in a season that felt over in June.
The moments that marked their ascent were many, an almost endless series of sliding doors and what ifs, minor-turned-monumental plays. Recently, in a series of interviews, some of these Sox reflected on their favorites.
“The fun thing about a season,” Durbin said, “is that there’s a whole lot of moments you can look back on that tell the story.”
The Schlitt Show
The date: June 25
The playoff odds (via FanGraphs): 10.6 percent
The moment: Caleb Durbin homers off Cam Schlittler
Remember how dire it felt on June 25. In the end, it was the start of the Red Sox’ run.
When Boston had last played at Fenway Park, it got swept by the Blue Jays, including a gut-wrenching finale in which the Sox rallied for a late tie only to lose. Emanating from the stands were loud boos and chants of “sell the team,” sentiments and sounds burned into the players’ psyche.
Just before they returned, the Sox dramatically dropped two of three to the Rockies. Durbin partially dislocated his left pinkie finger sliding head-first into first base. On the way back from Colorado, plane problems delayed their Boston arrival to 5 a.m., about 14 hours before the first pitch of a four-game series against the Yankees.
“And,” Isiah Kiner-Falefa said, “Schlittler.”
On the mound that night was righthander Cam Schlittler, the Walpole native and emerging Yankees ace, who ended the Red Sox’ season last year.
The weekend was ripe for misery. And it was the beginning of everything.
“It’s a very discernible line in the sand: the Yankees series at home,” interim manager Chad Tracy said.
The Red Sox were hitting like they had barely slept the night before, so Schlittler cruised into the fifth inning. But when a Yankees fielding error prolonged the frame, the Sox managed to tie it. Up came Durbin with the go-ahead run on base.
Durbin, back in the lineup a day after popping that pinkie back into place, homered to left field — just high enough and just far enough, off the lip of the Green Monster.
The dirt dog Durbin? Against that team, off that pitcher, after that travel and those losses?
“That was the big defining moment of the year,” Kiner-Falefa said. “Turned the whole attitude of the team around.”
The Red Sox trailed for half of an inning the rest of the series, sweeping all four games.
Still in a huge hole, they were 10 games under .500 at 36-46. But for the first time, they had something tangible to build on, not just blind belief.
“Right there is when it changed,” Tracy said. “Oh my God, that was awesome. But like, was that a blip? That’s what people think.”
The comeback
The date: July 12
The playoff odds: 40.5 percent
The moment: Francisco Lindor’s error leads to ninth consecutive win
Against the Angels, against the White Sox, after an overnight flight delay trying to escape Chicago, despite rolling up to Citi Field just two hours before scheduled first pitch, the Red Sox won eight consecutive games to take them into mid-July.
It was a significant accomplishment, especially considering it took them three months to win more than three in a row.
Unfortunately for the Sox, that is where the win streak was going to end. The Red Sox had one hit heading into the ninth inning against the Mets.
With a runner on first base and one out in the ninth, Romy Gonzalez hit a hard ground ball right at Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor. It was a ready-made double play. The game was over, and so was the streak … until it wasn’t.
“The guy has a Platinum Glove,” Whitlock said.
“Oh, now it’s our turn,” Connor Wong said. “Everything was going wrong for us, and then the one thing kind of went right for us.”
“He makes that play, we lose. And we somehow win that game,” Durbin said. “That was probably our biggest game of the year. Not because of who we beat, but because of the way we won that game.”
Lindor failed to turn the double play. He failed to get even one out. The ball ricocheted off his chest, everybody was safe, Devin Williams lost the strike zone, Durbin walked to load the bases, Andruw Monasterio walked to force in a run, and Jarren Duran singled to bring in the tying run. The Red Sox won in 10 innings.
Opportunity knocked, and the Red Sox kicked the door down. It was the difference between an 8-1 road trip, a solid week-plus with a total dud of a loss heading into the break ... and a stunning 9-0, feeling great going into four days off, with a chance to bring the momentum home.
If the win streak had ended at eight, would the Sox have won the next six after the break? Would they have grabbed such a strong hold on a wild-card spot? Would they have known what it felt like to stage late comebacks — the theme of their summer surge?
“Even that ninth inning, though, we needed five people to do the job, and they all did. That was the first time that happened,” Durbin said. “That kind of sparked the feeling of OK, we’re a team that if we need to get something going, we can.”
Tracy said: “Two weeks ago, we were pretty entrenched as the worst team in the American League. Now, we were holding a spot or were really close. I felt like that was — for the whole group — all right, we have turned this around and we have a legitimate chance now.”
The homecoming
The date: July 17-22
The playoff odds: 50.3 percent to 61 percent
The moment: “There’s so many,” Tracy said, leading to six more wins
Upon returning from the All-Star break, the Red Sox reached the chaotic, fever dream, how-is-this-possible portion of their turnaround.
Every game — four more wins against the Rays, then two against the Orioles — seemed to bring out a more electric version of Fenway Park than the one before.
For the Red Sox, that was the most gratifying. Their lowest low, several players said, wasn’t getting dumped in Denver. It was struggling in Boston and hearing it from the home crowds. They went 17-27 at Fenway in the first half.
How to pick just one moment?
For win No. 10, the first game back from the break, the Red Sox beat Tampa Bay, 10-0. It was resounding.
“That was like an important statement game for us,” Greg Weissert said.
For No. 11, the second game of a doubleheader, the Rays scored two runs in the top of the first and the Red Sox came right back with three in the bottom half. That got them back to .500 and into a tie for a playoff spot.
“Relentlessness,” Trevor Story said.
For No. 12, Wilyer Abreu’s fourth homer in two games was a go-ahead shot off Garrett Cleavinger, capping a four-run rally in the seventh for the Sox’ first lead of the day.
“When you win that many games in a row, there’s usually three or four of them that you’re probably not supposed to win,” Tracy said.
For No. 13, Sonny Gray tossed a quality start in an actual low-stress afternoon.
“It’s hard to remember everything,” Wong said.
For No. 14, Durbin went deep again, in the eighth against Tyler Wells to break a tie. Fourth-string shortstop Tsung-Che Cheng recorded the final out with a leaping catch of a line drive to save two runs.
Even for the Red Sox, the believers, it strained belief.
“It comes off the bat and you’re like, ‘Oh no.’ And [Cheng] out of nowhere snares it,” Tracy said. “Everybody’s fired up in the coach’s room and you fist bump. You shake your head like: ‘Holy [expletive]. We did it again.’ There were plenty of those for sure behind the scenes.”
For No. 15, they scored four runs in the first inning, leaving no doubt and matching the franchise record win streak set in 1946.
Later that day, July 22, the Red Sox lost the second game of a doubleheader. The streak was over — for real this time. The season is not.
That 15-0 run was part of 27-3 and 32-5 stretches, some of the wildest in franchise history.
“It was maybe the beginning of August, I think, when someone was like, ‘Hey, you realize we’re six games up in the wild card, right?’” said Whitlock, not a standings tracker. “Wait, what?”
“That’s a testament to the people that we have,” Durbin said. “As a player, we have talent. We have a lot of talent to do the job. But [after] the start we had, it takes the person to continue to push forward and come out of it the way we did.”
“I never doubted it, our ability to come together at some point and turn this thing around,” interim bench coach José David Flores said. “To be honest with you, it was kind of shocking the way we did it.”

(Photo credit: Erik Williams)
Mike Yastrzemski capped a four-run sixth inning with a three-run homer, and the visiting Atlanta Braves clinched the National League East with a 4-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Sunday.
The Braves swept the three-game interleague series and claimed their seventh division pennant over the last nine seasons. Yastrzemski was the last of four batters to reach safely against Astros left-handed reliever Bryan King (3-6), who didn't record a single out and exited after allowing Yastrzemski's 12th homer of the season.
Jose Altuve and Yainer Diaz homered for the spiraling Astros, who will enter the final week of the regular season one game behind the Texas Rangers in the American League West.
Astros starter Hunter Brown allowed just three singles and two walks over five shutout innings. Braves starter Martin Perez navigated traffic, allowing just one run on six hits and two walks in 4 1/3 innings.
Rays 5, Red Sox 1
Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in two runs apiece during a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays defeated visiting Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
With the win, the Rays completed their final regular-season homestand with an 8-1 record and wrapped their home schedule with a major league-best 55-26 mark.
Trevor Story homered, and Roman Anthony and Caleb Durbin each went 2-for-4 for the Red Sox, who managed just six hits while losing their second straight game.
Pirates 4, Royals 3
Rafael Flores Jr. belted a go-ahead two-run homer in the eighth inning to cap Pittsburgh's three-game sweep over visiting Kansas City. With the win, the Pirates improved to 14-6 in their last 20 games.
Oneil Cruz went deep to lead off the fourth inning and Spencer Horwitz had an RBI single in the sixth for Pittsburgh. Carmen Mlodzinski earned the win after allowing two runs on three hits in three innings.
Vinnie Pasquantino had a pinch-hit two-run homer for the Royals, who have lost four in a row and seven of their past eight games.
Phillies 7, Mets 2
Cristopher Sanchez tossed 6 1/3 solid innings and earned the victory for visiting Philadelphia, which earned a much-needed win over New York.
Luis Arraez was 1-for-4 with two RBIs for the Phillies. Justin Crawford provided insurance in the eighth with a bases-clearing triple off Kodai Senga. Sanchez (18-6) gave up two runs on six hits. Philadelphia sits four games ahead of the Arizona Diamondbacks in the race for the final National League wild card.
Bo Bichette homered for the Mets, who dropped their home finale for the third time in four years, while Brett Baty had a pinch-hit run-scoring single in the seventh. Francisco Alvarez and A.J. Ewing each singled twice.
Cubs 9, Reds 1
Pete Crow-Armstrong tied the major league lead with his 45th home run, and David Peterson held host Cincinnati to one run on three hits in six innings in Chicago's win.
Crow-Armstrong was 3-for-5 with two RBIs, three runs, his 30th double and his 38th stolen base. He matched Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber at 45 homers, and he became the first center fielder in history with 40 home runs, 30 doubles and 30 steals in a season.
Michael Conforto and Seiya Suzuki also homered for the Cubs. JJ Bleday hit a home run for the Reds, who have dropped three of four.
Cardinals 5, Nationals 3
Leo Bernal's two-run home run capped a three-run eighth inning, and St. Louis rallied for a win against visiting Washington to salvage the finale of the three-game series.
Ivan Herrera tied it 3-3 with one out when he hit his second solo homer of the day. Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless inning for the win. Jose Fermin had two hits for the Cardinals, who had lost four straight.
CJ Abrams homered, and Daylen Lile had a double and a single for Washington, which had won six of seven.
Mariners 2, Rockies 1
Kade Anderson threw seven scoreless innings, allowing just three hits in the longest outing of his rookie season, and visiting Seattle stayed alive in the postseason race with a win over Colorado in Denver.
Dominic Canzone had two hits and two RBIs for Seattle, which gained a game on the Texas Rangers in the AL West. Closer Andres Munoz left the game in the ninth with an apparent right arm injury.
Hunter Goodman's 39th home run of the season couldn't prevent Colorado from moving within one loss of its fourth consecutive 100-loss season.
Blue Jays 7, Rangers 2
Nathan Lukes and Charles McAdoo each had two RBIs to lead Toronto to a win over Texas in Arlington, Texas.
Kazuma Okamoto broke a 2-2 deadlock with an RBI single in the fifth and gave the Blue Jays a lead they would never relinquish as they remained three games back of the final AL wild-card spot. Spencer Arrighetti (9-9) picked up the win, allowing two runs in 2 1/3 innings during a bullpen game.
Jake Burger delivered the Rangers' lone runs on a game-tying two-run homer in the fourth. Jacob deGrom (11-10) had a shaky outing, giving up three runs with five hits in 4 1/3 innings for Texas, which maintained its one-game lead in the AL West despite the defeat.
Brewers 3, Orioles 0
Jacob Misiorowski set the tone with three shutout innings and Milwaukee blanked host Baltimore for the second game in a row to complete a three-game sweep and set a franchise record for regular-season victories.
William Contreras homered, and Cooper Pratt provided two run-scoring singles with two outs. Milwaukee is two games ahead of the Los Angeles Dodgers for the best record in the National League. Misiorowski's ERA dipped to 1.86.
The Orioles further damaged their fading playoff hopes, losing the first three games of the homestand to fall five games back of the Chicago White Sox for the final American League wild-card spot. Colton Cowser had two of Baltimore's four hits. Orioles starter Brandon Young (9-5) was charged with two runs in six innings.
Diamondbacks 8, Yankees 4
Nolan Arenado hit his third grand slam of the season to cap a five-run fifth and Arizona kept its slim National League wild-card chances alive with a victory over New York in Phoenix.
Geraldo Perdomo had two hits and two RBIs and five Arizona relievers limited the Yankees to three hits in 6 1/3 scoreless innings. The D-backs remained five games behind NL wild-card leaders Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four behind the Philadelphia Phillies with six to play.
Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones homered for the Yankees, who fell six games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East. The Yankees lead the American League with 216 homers. Lombard had two hits.
Twins 8, Angels 0
Dean Kremer allowed one hit over six innings and Alan Roden went 3-for-5 with a home run and four RBIs as Minnesota earned a split of its four-game series with Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Josh Bell had three hits, a walk, two RBIs and a run while Brooks Lee also had three hits and scored three times for Minnesota, which finished with 13 hits. Kremer (4-5) allowed just a fourth-inning leadoff single to Vaughn Grissom.
Ryan Johnson (5-9) suffered the loss for Los Angeles, which finished the 2026 season with a 34-47 home record.
Guardians 1, Athletics 0
Gavin Williams threw seven shutout innings to lift Cleveland past the visiting Athletics.
Williams (14-8) gave up only three hits while throwing 63 of 89 pitches for strikes. Steven Kwan had three hits and Cade Smith earned his 39th save as the Guardians swept the series and remain atop the American League Central.
A's starter Jack Perkins (3-12) gave up five hits and one run in six innings. Zack Gelof had two of the team's six hits as the Athletics suffered their sixth straight loss
Dodgers 3, Giants 1
Emmet Sheehan pitched brilliantly in long relief, Enrique Hernandez broke a seventh-inning tie with a run-scoring double and Los Angeles completed a three-game sweep of visiting San Francisco.
Tommy Edman homered for the Dodgers, who trailed 1-0 after one inning before Sheehan took over to start the second and held the Giants to just one hit with nine strikeouts over the next 5 1/3 scoreless innings.
Jung Hoo Lee and Victor Bericoto singled for the only hits for the Giants, who completed their road schedule with a 28-53 record. Sam Hentges (1-7) allowed a pair of one-out singles in the seventh before Hernandez's double for a 2-1 edge.
Padres 7, Marlins 3
Jake Cronenworth homered twice and knocked in a season-high five runs while Fernando Tatis Jr. also homered as host San Diego polished off a three-game sweep and finished 6-0 against Miami this season.
The Padres won their fifth straight game and are 13-1 in their last 14 games. Walker Buehler (9-6) worked 6 2/3 innings, allowing three hits and three runs.
Sandy Alcantara (13-11) absorbed the loss for the Marlins after permitting eight hits and four runs over six innings. Alcantara is winless in his last eight starts.
White Sox 8, Tigers 1
Chase Meidroth hit a two-run homer for Chicago and Sam Antonacci's two-run double highlighted a 2-for-4 performance as the White Sox waited through a rain delay of nearly four hours and played in wet, blustery conditions to beat Detroit.
Five pitchers held the Tigers to six hits and five walks as Detroit was limited to a single run for the third time in the series. Huascar Brazoban (6-2), reinstated prior to the game from the 15-day injured list (left lat strain), pitched for the first time since Aug. 24. He allowed a hit in one inning to get his first victory with the White Sox.
Tigers starter Troy Melton (8-5) allowed four runs in 3 2/3 innings, giving up four hits before exiting with a trainer. Detroit pitchers allowed eight walks, with White Sox third baseman Miguel Vargas (1-for-2) drawing three of them. Eduardo Valencia went 3-for-4 for the Tigers, who were eliminated from postseason contention.
--Field Level Media

As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox.
The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are 9-9 this month, struggling offensively, without on several injured stars, and are their first postseason round will almost certainly be a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where they fell to their rivals 2-1.
In other words, there is much work to be done. The Red Sox know it, and they are eager to prove they did not come this far to only go this far.
“This has been a turbulent season,” Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow told reporters. “This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here.”
But neither the recent struggles nor the battles ahead should diminish the magnitude of the overall achievement of getting to this point.
The Red Sox lost American League Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet to a shoulder injury in mid-April, and he has yet to return.
They fired manager Alex Cora and several coaches in the middle of a late-April road series in Baltimore, and promoted Triple-A Worcester skipper Chad Tracy and several others from their minor league coaching ranks.
Injuries sidelined star outfielder Roman Anthony and veteran shortstop Trevor Story from early May until the very end of August.
The Red Sox owned their worst home record to start a season since 1932, and were 15 1/2 games out of first in the American League East in June.
On June 24, they fell to 14 games under .500. On Sunday, they became the fourth team in Major League Baseball history to go from as many as 14 games under .500 to the postseason in the same season.
“We needed time, and the time came for us,” veteran first baseman Willson Contreras told his teammates in the clubhouse. “I’m very proud of you all.”
“It’s 162 for a reason,” echoed third baseman Caleb Durbin.
“Obviously, getting where we want to go, but ultimately, what we had to overcome to get here makes it all the more sweet,” Tracy said. “We had a long way to go, and they never stopped, and they didn’t take no for an answer.”
This year looked lost, and the Red Sox managed to save it. They maintained an unshakeable belief in themselves, and it has already taken them to places most of the baseball world doubted it could go.
“Belief, belief, belief,” Contreras told reporters. “That was my main word, and that’s what I did from Day 1.”
The Red Sox are not a perfect team. But they certainly have the grit and gumption to go further than expected, as evidenced by the fact that they have already done so by reaching this point.
“We know how it felt when we left New York at the end of the year,” Story said. “You know how it made me feel. So that stayed with me.”
“They came together, and they found a way to get it done, and they had a long way to go to do it,” Tracy said. “They’re very battle-tested, and I’m super, super proud of them.”
“We don’t care where we play,” Tracy said. “You go back to July, and most people didn’t think we’d even be standing here. So it doesn’t matter where we play.”
“We’re in,” Tracy continued. “You got a ticket to the dance, and now you got to go take care of it there.”
“We’re in, baby,” Story said. “Let’s go.”
“Now, this is the moment,” right-fielder Wilyer Abreu said, “that we (were) waiting for.”

AL-best Rays complete 8-1 homestand by stifling Red Sox
(Photo credit: Pablo Robles)
Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in a pair apiece in a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays won for the eighth time in their final regular-season homestand by beating the Boston Red Sox 5-1 on Sunday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
In finishing 8-1 on their last homestand before the postseason, the Rays (95-60) sent nine batters to the plate in the first and never looked back as they concluded their home schedule with a majors-best 55-26 mark.
Starter Griffin Jax (8-10) fired five scoreless frames with three hits allowed. He fanned five with two walks over 74 offerings.
Trevor Story homered, and Roman Anthony (double) and Caleb Durbin each went 2-for-4. However, Boston (84-72) managed only six hits in losing its second straight.
Starter Patrick Sandoval (1-7) rebounded from a terrible beginning to finish seven innings, allowing five runs on four hits. He struck out five, walked two and hit a batter in 94 pitches.
Tampa Bay put its first five batters on base against Sandoval, and DeLuca doubled in two runs before Simpson singled in two more as the Rays batted around in the first.
Jax was dialed in early after yielding a leadoff single to Anthony. The right-hander retired 10 straight batters, four by strikeouts, until Adley Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth.
In the bottom of the fourth, Mesa made it 5-0 by cranking Sandoval's 95 mph four-seamer out to right-center a Statcast-estimated 403 feet. It was the right fielder's 14th home run.
The Red Sox had a chance to get back in it by loading the bases in the fifth on a single by Durbin and two walks, but Anthony -- who drove in five of the club's six runs in the series -- whiffed to end it on a sinking 2-2 changeup from Jax, the starter's final pitch.
With a fire alarm going off behind center field causing a short delay, Cole Sulser tossed a perfect sixth as the bullpen began its stretch of four innings of one-run work.
Story hit his fifth homer with one out in the ninth to spoil the shutout.
--Field Level Media

The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways.
They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs.
A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on back-to-back two-run base hits by centerfielder Jonny DeLuca (double) and left-fielder Chandler Simpson (single) before the Red Sox starter could record an out. Sandoval issued his second walk of the inning to Victor Mesa Jr. before he finished the frame and stranded two runners.
“Nightmare, like legit nightmare situation,” a grimacing Sandoval told reporters postgame of the first inning. “Couldn’t really where my arm was in space, grip on the ball wasn’t great. Just a literal nightmare.”
Then came a complete 180. Sandoval looked like a new man when he returned for the bottom of the second. He set the Rays down in order on eight pitches, then needed six to do so again in the third.
Sandoval retired eight consecutive Rays before Mesa homered with one out in the fourth to push the lead to five. But it marked Tampa Bay’s fourth and final hit of the day; Sandoval retired his last 11 batters, and newly-returned righty Tyron Guerrero extended the streak to 14 with a 1-2-3 eighth.
Yet the Red Sox, who left 17 men on base over the first two games of the series, were blanked by righty Griffin Jax and the Rays bullpen until a brief rally bid in the top of the ninth. Boston out-hit Tampa Bay 6-4, but went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position, and stranded six.
Roman Anthony led off the game with a groundball single to right, but he was erased and replaced when catcher Adley Rutschman popped into a force out. The Red Sox did not put another man on base until Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth, an opportunity quickly erased by shortstop Trevor Story grounding into an inning-ending double play.
Boston’s best chance came and went in Jax’s fifth and final frame, when they loaded the bases on a one-out single by third baseman Caleb Durbin, and walks to centerfielder Jarren Duran and right-fielder Nate Eaton. Jax, who had not exceeded 67 pitches in a start since Aug. 2, was up to 69 when Anthony came to bat with two outs and the bases loaded. It took five pitches to end the threat; Anthony swung and missed at Jax’s last two, a 95.3 mph sinker and 90.2 mph changeup.
Much like Saturday’s 2-1 loss, Boston had no hope against the Tampa Bay bullpen. The Red Sox went in order against Cole Sulser in the sixth, and Brody Hopkins in the seventh.
Facing 2025 Red Sox trade deadline acquisition Steven Matz in the eighth, Anthony doubled with two outs. Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for designated hitter Mickey Gasper. Jones has dominated left-handed pitching since the Red Sox acquired him from the Detroit Tigers during the All-Star break, but Matz struck him out swinging on four pitches.
After his 40-pitch first, Sandoval completed his remaining six innings on a mere 54. He became just the fourth Red Sox pitcher in the last 26 years, and first since Rick Porcello in 2016, to pitch at least seven innings after giving up at least four runs in the first. Sandoval yielded five earned runs on four hits, walked two (both in the first), and struck out five over seven innings. He threw 73.4% of his 94 pitches for strikes.
Activated from the injured list Sunday morning, Guerrero was sharp in his first inning of work since Aug. 31. The towering righty retired the Rays’ No. 2-4 batters, including American League home-run leader Junior Caminero, in order on 12 pitches (nine strikes). Guerrero’s return will bolster a Boston bullpen currently without closer Aroldis Chapman (day-to-day with lat tightness), and righty Justin Slaten (season-ending flexor injury).
Story ensured the Red Sox would not be shut out. His fifth home run of the year, off righty Ty Johnson, soared 405 feet to left at 102.7 mph with one out in the ninth.
Thus concludes the final Red Sox road trip of the season. They went 2-4 against the Texas Rangers and Rays, were outscored 23-15, and left 42 men on base.
After an off-day Monday, their final homestand of the season begins Tuesday night against the Cleveland Guardians.
But first, all eyes turn to the Braves and Astros.
